MC: A student helped coordinate a school event. Which résumé note gives the clearest evidence for an employer who needs reliable record handling?

column3: “I am naturally organized.”
“My friends trust me.”
“I checked sign-up names against the supply list and asked the teacher about one mismatch.”
“I want a job with records.”

MC: It names a relevant task, action, and safe response to uncertainty. The other statements are preferences or unsupported labels.
A career profile says a certificate is commonly preferred; an Alberta regulator lists a credential as required for a protected title. What should the student verify before planning training?

column3: Whether the exact job title is regulated and which current requirement applies.
Whether the shortest program uses the word “career.”
Whether classmates think the certificate is useful.
Whether the profile has a photo of the workplace.

MC: The exact role and current regulator requirement control the credential question; a profile preference and a regulated-title requirement are different.
A program route costs a fictional $1,600 tuition, $240 tools, and $35 monthly transit for 8 months. What is the listed total for these items?
$1,600 + $240 + (8 × $35) = $2,120. This is only the stated fictional cost set.
An Alberta career report gives a five-year projection. A local search today finds two postings. Which conclusion is best supported?

column3: The projection guarantees a local opening for this student.
The local search proves the provincial report is false.
The two sources measure different things; record their dates, locations, and definitions before comparing.
The student should average the two counts.

MC: A projection and a one-day vacancy search are not directly comparable; context and definitions matter.
A student cannot take a prerequisite course in the planned semester. What is the most useful next step?

column3: Assume any similar course will count.
Abandon the long-term interest immediately.
Ignore the prerequisite and submit the plan as complete.
Ask the school about the next offering or approved equivalent, then update the route and timing.

MC: Confirm the sequence and approved options before revising; an availability constraint can change timing without deciding the goal.
A fictional job posting requires greeting visitors and protecting their information. Which example best supports both needs?

column3: “At a school event I welcomed families and asked the coordinator before sharing a participant list.”
“I like talking and technology.”
“I am an expert in privacy law.”
“My cousin is good with people.”

MC: It shows relevant communication and a permission-aware action without overstating expertise.
Which statement treats a career interest survey responsibly?

column3: Its top result proves which job the student should choose.
Use the result to generate roles, then compare tasks, training, and conditions.
Ignore all results because surveys are useless.
Choose the result with the highest salary.

MC: A survey can suggest hypotheses but cannot decide fit or replace occupational research.
A learner’s plan assumes a bus arrives exactly on time and fills every evening. Which revision improves feasibility?

column3: Add another course to strengthen the plan.
Assume motivation prevents delays.
Add travel and transition time plus a buffer, then check fixed commitments.
Remove rest to protect study time.

MC: A realistic schedule accounts for travel, transitions, fixed commitments, and recovery.
A fictional job requires a safety orientation before equipment use. The supervisor is away and a coworker says “just try it.” What should the learner do?

column3: Wait and ask an authorized supervisor for required instruction before using it.
Use the equipment carefully without orientation.
Copy another worker without asking.
Watch a video on a personal phone and begin.

MC: The missing training and authorization are a safety boundary; do not improvise.
Which interview response best answers “Tell me about a time plans changed”?

column3: “When a volunteer cancelled, I reassigned check-in, updated the schedule, and we opened on time.”
“I am adaptable.”
“My team was disorganized.”
“I always solve every problem.”

MC: The response gives a specific change, action, and result without relying on a broad claim.
A worker is unsure whether a shift is permitted for their age and task. What should they record before checking the current Alberta rule?

column3: Only the supervisor’s first name.
A rule from another province.
Their opinion about whether it feels fair.
Age, type of work, actual hours/time, and relevant workplace context.

MC: Applicability may depend on age, work, time, and other context; current Alberta guidance should then be consulted.
A bottle with no label is left beside a sink. Which action uses the worker’s safety rights appropriately?

column3: Smell it to identify it.
Mix a small amount with another cleaner.
Move it to a drain.
Pause, keep clear if safe, and ask for hazard information and training before handling it.

MC: The worker has a right to know about hazards and should not expose themselves while identifying an unknown substance.
A worker reports that a machine guard is loose. What is the strongest report?

column3: “The machine is bad.”
“At closing, the guard moved during inspection; I stopped using it and need the approved check before resuming.”
“The operator is careless.”
“Everyone should know better.”

MC: It states an observable condition, context, safe action, and needed follow-up.
A student sees a difference in who received training but has only one short note about it. What is a careful next step?

column3: Declare a legal finding immediately.
Post the names of all workers online.
Record dates, criteria, comparable roles, and exact statements, then seek appropriate support.
Delete the note because it is incomplete.

MC: A careful record separates facts from conclusions and supports timely advice without exposing private information.
A role profile and one current job posting describe different daily tasks. What should the learner do?

column3: Assume one source is lying.
Compare role scope, employer, date, and specialty; treat the posting as one opening.
Average the task lists.
Ignore the posting because profiles are always complete.

MC: The sources may cover different scopes; identify what each actually describes.
Which note is the best basis for revising a career hypothesis after a simulated shift?

column3: “I failed at work.”
“I will never use equipment.”
“The supervisor’s opinion decides my career.”
“I kept visitor details private, but delayed reporting a printer blocker; I will compare roles and practise earlier updates.”

MC: It connects observed actions to a specific, testable next step without turning one task into a permanent label.
Using the fictional profile below, compare two possible routes to a career direction. State one entry requirement to verify, two cost/time factors, and one reason to keep a backup route.
A fictional learner is interested in health work, prefers predictable hours, and is unsure about direct patient contact. Describe a three-step research plan that preserves choice and uses evidence.
A youth worker’s schedule, time record, and pay statement do not agree. Explain how to investigate the discrepancy and where to seek help without claiming a legal violation from incomplete facts.
In a fictional workplace case, an unidentified liquid is near a blocked exit and a supervisor is not immediately available. Write a safe response and explain which information you still need.
